title: What causes the seasons?
description: Earth’s tilt changes the angle of sunlight and the length of our days. Here’s why summer arrives at different times in each hemisphere.

sections.title: It starts with Earth’s tilt
sections.html:
It seems reasonable to think that summer happens when Earth moves closer to the Sun. But that would leave a puzzle: why is June summer in the Northern Hemisphere and winter in the Southern Hemisphere?

The main reason is Earth’s tilted axis. As Earth travels around the Sun, one hemisphere tilts towards it, receiving more direct sunlight and longer days. About six months later, the other hemisphere tilts towards the Sun.

sections.title: More direct light and longer days
sections.html:
Sunlight arriving at a low angle spreads over a larger area than sunlight striking more directly. In summer, a hemisphere receives more direct sunlight and has more daylight hours in which to warm up.

Earth’s distance from the Sun does change during the year. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in January, during Northern Hemisphere winter. That is a useful clue that distance alone cannot explain the seasons.

sections.title: Why the hemispheres have opposite seasons
sections.html:
When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, the Southern Hemisphere tilts away. One gets longer days and more direct sunlight while the other gets shorter days and less direct light.

Which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun during Northern Hemisphere summer?

The Northern Hemisphere. At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away.

sections.title: Notice the change where you live
sections.html:
Over several weeks, you may notice daylight lasting longer or shadows changing at the same time of day. Those everyday changes are a way to see the seasonal pattern for yourself.

A cold summer afternoon or a mild winter day can still happen. Weather varies from day to day; the seasons describe a much longer cycle.
